A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HSBC research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Original appendices A–E can be matched across versions; v3 adds Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-learning experiments on six simulated control tasks, including learning curves, numerical comparisons, and three hyperparameter ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds comparator evaluations, reward-correlation analysis, alternative feedback-model tests, an ensemble-size ablation, and experiments with four human volunteers.

M1.justification: The core reward model, voting cuts, conservative threshold, optimization, filtering, and MPC procedure are retained. However, Section 6.4 replaces explicitly pairing a new segment with a buffered segment with randomly pairing mixed new/old segments. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the sampling procedure or merely compresses its description.

E1.justification: The same six control tasks are retained. Sections 7.5–7.6 add Stoc, Mistake, and Myopic feedback scenarios on Cartpole and feedback from four real human volunteers on Cartpole and Walker. These substantially extend feedback sources and test conditions beyond v1's simulated batchwise label flips.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates a PEBBLE-derived baseline alongside HSBC and the oracle. v3 adds RIME, SURF, and PEBBLE variants using MAE and t-CE losses to Cartpole and Walker comparisons at 20% and 30% false preferences (Table 2 and Appendix F). These are newly evaluated comparators, including methods previously only cited.

E3.justification: New protocols include simulated-feedback bootstrapping followed by human feedback with conservativeness set to 40%, specified B-Pref teacher parameters, and Pearson-correlation evaluation using five 200-step trajectories. Appendix F specifies MPPI adaptations for added baselines and SURF's 60-step segments cropped to 50. The original architecture, optimizer settings, and MPPI parameter tables are retained.

E4.justification: v3 retains the conservativeness, disagreement-threshold, and batch-size ablations, and adds ensemble sizes of 4, 8, 16, and 32. It also adds learned-versus-ground-truth reward correlation analysis and robustness tests across feedback models, exposing difficulty with the stochastic teacher. These examine substantially more aspects of reliability than v1.

E5.justification: Section 7.4 adds Pearson-correlation estimation from five 200-step trajectories, reporting the mean and standard deviation of those estimates. Existing experiments retain five independent training runs, five evaluation runs, and mean/standard-deviation reporting. There is no stated increase in those run counts or addition of significance tests.

E6.justification: The original DM-Control entries in Table 1 are retained. New results include 10% and 30% noise conditions for dexterous manipulation and Go2, additional comparator scores, reward correlations, ensemble-size sensitivity, and human-feedback curves. New Cartpole teacher-specific rewards are 93.6 for Stoc, 122.6 for Mistake, and 127.0 for Myopic (Table 4).

T1.justification: Section 4.2 corrects the Heaviside definition for negative inputs from 1 to 0, making it consistent with the stated voting interpretation. The lemmas, Theorem 4.2, and proofs in Appendices D–E are substantively retained. The added neural-network VC-dimension discussion explains applicability rather than establishing a new theorem.

C1.justification: Both versions claim geometrically interpretable, query-efficient reward alignment with provable robustness and favorable performance under erroneous preferences. v3 emphasizes avoiding explicit identification of false preferences in the abstract, but v1 already states this contribution in Section 2.2. Added experiments strengthen support without redefining the core claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds localized qualifications: it attributes stochastic-teacher difficulty to noisy labels when trajectory rewards become similar, explicitly excludes tied preferences, discusses treating conservativeness as a constant hyperparameter, and explains portability costs without GPU acceleration. These extend applicability and failure-condition discussion while retaining the central mechanism interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a paper/code access link and Appendix F with comparator adaptations, RIME and SURF hyperparameters, segment-cropping instructions, and robust-loss specifications. Appendix C also clarifies which existing batch budgets apply at 10% and 30% noise. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained main experimental settings.

R1.justification: Related work adds CANDERE-COACH and Uni-RLHF, and revises RIME's description from discriminator training to KL-based filtering and label flipping. New citations support robust-loss baselines and neural-network VC dimensions. The overall positioning against preference learning and hypothesis-space methods remains intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

P1.justification: v3 copyedits and clarifies passages throughout, shortens task names, corrects the running header, and updates author information. It adds experimental subsections and Appendix F while preserving the main section sequence and original appendix organization. The accompanying prose changes do not amount to a wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v1's separate task learning-curve figures and result tables are consolidated and expanded into v3's Figure 5 and Table 1. The ablation display grows from three to four panels. New Tables 2–4, human-feedback Figure 7, and comparator Figure 9 substantially expand the empirical presentation; the conceptual illustrations are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness claim through direct comparisons with robust competitors, alternative feedback models, and four-volunteer human tests, addressing v1's reliance on one PEBBLE-style baseline and simulated flips. It also discloses stochastic-teacher failure and expands implementation information. The human study remains small and simulation-bootstrapped, but the gain in validation is substantial.
